summary:
Israel's electoral map is sorted by sector, religiosity and socio-economic status (SES) far more than by region, and locality targeting should start from that. Some groups are effectively lost to the Change bloc: Haredi localities (97% coalition in 2022) and settlements east of the separation barrier (about 60% RZP). The Change bloc's base is secular, high-SES Jews: 74% of secular voters backed the opposition, and every cluster 8-10 city chose Blue and White in 2019. These places already turn out near their ceiling (about 75% in clusters 8-10 against about 61% in clusters 2-4), so getting more voters out there yields little.

The persuadable core is 'traditional' Jews. They gave the coalition 66.5% in 2022, but the traditional non-religious subgroup gave about 31% to Yesh Atid and National Unity. They are concentrated in mid-cluster (5-7) central and coastal cities. Those cities match the national result most closely: Rehovot, Petah Tikva, Haifa, Hadera, Netanya, Holon, Rosh HaAyin. Pluralities flipped there in 2019-2020: Likud gained 5-9 points in its strongholds and overtook Blue and White in Rishon LeZion and Rosh HaAyin.

Development towns are Likud strongholds with low, swinging turnout, and Likud's final-day turnout drive targets them (Beit She'an, Tiberias, Dimona, Kiryat Gat, Afula, Ariel). Raising turnout there helps Netanyahu. The Change bloc should persuade there, not get out the vote, using local, place-based messages on neglect of the north, the Haredi draft and cost of living.

The 2022 defeat came mostly from turnout gaps plus wasted votes, not from voters switching sides. Turnout rose 3-7 points in right-wing strongholds and only about 0.3 points in centre-left cities, and roughly 9% of votes went to lists below the threshold. 2026 polling reverses that enthusiasm gap: 80% of opposition supporters say they are certain to vote, against 72% of coalition supporters.

Druze localities are a high-return target. About 70% of their vote went to parties now in or close to the Change bloc, turnout is only about 49% (it was 76-79% in 1996-99), and the vote moves sharply toward any party with a Druze candidate in a winnable list slot. That party usually wins the candidate's home village, with a home-village bonus of roughly 30-50 points. Druze anger over the Nation-State Law and the Kaminitz law adds to the opening. Risks:
- Blue and White's Druze candidate could waste votes below the threshold.
- Druze voters may drift toward Netanyahu after the 2025 Sweida crisis.

Arab localities give Zionist parties only about 14%. The Negev Bedouin vote 74% for Ra'am, and turnout at their tribal polling stations is 38%. Both matter mainly in the scenario where Ra'am is part of the governing majority, and third-party transport to the polls is legally restricted.

The research on war shocks points both ways:
- Rocket and terror exposure has historically moved localities 1-6 points to the right.
- Soldiers who served in a badly managed war later punished the governing party.
- In 2026 the Haifa and Northern districts favour the opposition 38 to 26, while 65% say the state is abandoning the north. Likud's candidate came second in Kiryat Shmona's 2025 municipal race.

Displacement is a turnout risk. Fewer than half of Kiryat Shmona's residents were living there in April 2026. About 90% of Gaza-envelope residents have returned, but kibbutzim such as Be'eri, Nir Oz and Kfar Aza remain largely empty.

On field practice:
- Parties legally receive the voter register, and register-based apps that track support station by station (e.g. Elector) are standard.
- Likud runs a machine that targets its strongholds, with last-minute 'gevalt' alarm calls about low turnout.
- Double-envelope votes, cast by soldiers and reservists away from home, cannot be assigned to localities.

Caveat: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through, so several requested strands are thin or missing (see open questions).

findings.claim: A study of all 1,215 Jewish and Arab localities in 2022 found that higher socio-economic status predicts higher turnout in both sectors, and larger localities have lower turnout. Development towns turn out less, while settlements and Haredi localities turn out more. Distance from the centre does not predict turnout in Jewish and mixed localities but does in Arab ones.
findings.quant: National turnout about 70%; 1,215 localities; 8 socio-demographic and geographic predictors tested (the abstract gives no coefficients).
findings.authors: Nir Atmor, Chen Friedberg, Liran Harsgor
findings.title: For Whom the Polls Toll? Voter Turnout in the 2022 Elections
findings.venue: The Elections in Israel 2022 (eds. Rahat, Gidron, Shamir), Routledge/Taylor & Francis, pp. 67-88
findings.relevance: Specify the turnout-headroom model as expected turnout = f(SES cluster, log size, sector, development-town flag, settlement flag, Haredi share) and compute headroom per locality as the gap between expected and actual turnout. Development-town headroom is mostly Likud upside, so weight it by the Change bloc's net share before treating it as a target.

findings.claim: Turnout in Israeli localities rises with the CBS socio-economic cluster, and the gap has persisted for decades. In non-Haredi Jewish localities, the top clusters (8-10) consistently turn out well above the low-middle clusters (2-4).
findings.quant: 2013, non-Haredi Jewish localities: clusters 8-10 74.5%, clusters 2-4 60.7%, clusters 1-2 51.6% (one locality). 1996: 86.3% vs 81.8%. Survey: 17.7% of 18-22-year-olds said they would not vote, against about 9% of those over 50.
findings.authors: Ella Heller (IDI), summarising Afriat & Dahan (2010) with 2013 data
findings.title: Who Doesn't Vote in the Israeli Knesset Elections?
findings.relevance: Supports a 10-18 point SES turnout gap. The Change bloc's high-SES base is near its turnout ceiling, so its own get-out-the-vote headroom lies mainly in young voters and middle clusters (5-7), not cluster 9-10 suburbs.

findings.topic: 2022 outcome: differential turnout and wasted votes
findings.claim: IDI's results analysis found turnout rose clearly in right-wing strongholds (development towns, big southern cities, Haredim, Jerusalem) compared with 2021, but stayed flat or fell slightly in centre-left strongholds (Tel Aviv, kibbutzim). The two blocs were nearly tied in votes, and lists below the threshold decided the seat result.
findings.quant: Netanyahu bloc ahead by about 30,000 votes; almost 9% of votes wasted below the threshold (about 300,000 for Meretz and Balad); Arab turnout 53.2%.
findings.title: The 2022 Elections: Results Analysis
findings.relevance: The model's impact score should value (a) differential turnout in the Change bloc's own strongholds and (b) keeping Change-bloc lists above the threshold, rather than raw persuasion alone.

findings.claim: Turnout rose most in right-leaning cities and barely moved in centre-left cities, which widened the right's margin. Arab turnout recovered from its 2021 low, while the share of Arab voters choosing Zionist parties has collapsed over three decades.
findings.quant: Turnout change 2021 to 2022: Dimona +6.9, Beersheba +4.6, Ashkelon +3.2, Tel Aviv +0.4, Givatayim +0.3, Herzliya +0.3 points. National turnout 67.4% to 70.6%. Arab turnout 44.6% to 53.2%. Right bloc 48.3% to 49.6%; centre-left 41.5% to 38.3%. Arab votes for Zionist parties: 52.3% in 1992, 14.2% in 2022.
findings.title: The Israeli Electorate from the Perspective of the 2022 Elections (INSS Insight No. 1664)
findings.relevance: Use these figures to set how far turnout can swing between elections by locality type: about 3-7 points in Likud-leaning mid-size cities, under 1 point in saturated centre-left cities.

findings.topic: Swing localities: Likud stronghold mobilisation, 2019 to 2020
findings.claim: Between September 2019 and March 2020, Likud gained 5-9 points of vote share in its peripheral and southern strongholds while Blue and White stayed flat everywhere. Likud overtook Blue and White in the mid-cluster central cities of Rishon LeZion and Rosh HaAyin, and Netanyahu issued election-day alarms about low turnout in Likud bastions.
findings.quant: Likud share Sept 2019 to Mar 2020: Sderot 42.1 to 51.2; Kiryat Gat 37.2 to 45.7; Ashkelon 40.5 to 48.1; Netanya 35.9 to 43.1; Beersheba 43.4 to 50.1; Ashdod 31.2 to 36.6. Rishon LeZion: Likud 33.9 to 40.2 vs Blue and White 36.6 to 36.9. Rosh HaAyin: Likud 34.6 to 40.2 vs Blue and White 34.7 to 35.1. Likud seats 32 to 36.
findings.title: Polls apart: Likud boosted turnout where it needed to as Blue and White stalled
findings.relevance: Mid-cluster central cities (Rishon LeZion, Rosh HaAyin, Netanya, Ashdod, Petah Tikva) are where pluralities actually flip. Give them a high swing weight and calibrate locality swing variance at about 5-9 points between consecutive elections.

findings.claim: In the last campaign day of 2022, Likud concentrated on mobilising turnout in its bastions rather than persuading new voters, betting that the usual enthusiasm gap favouring the left could be closed.
findings.quant: Named target towns: Beit She'an, Tiberias, Dimona, Tirat Carmel, Kiryat Gat, Afula, Ariel; Likud won about 50% of valid votes there in 2021.
findings.title: It all boils down to turnout: parties focus on key strongholds in last day of campaign
findings.relevance: Expect Netanyahu-bloc turnout operations in these towns. The Change bloc should not raise general turnout there; if it acts at all, it should run persuasion on issues like the draft and periphery neglect. It should mirror the tactic by mobilising its own strongholds and mixed-profile cities.

findings.topic: Religiosity and bloc vote (who is persuadable)
findings.claim: Religious self-definition is the strongest single sorter of Jewish votes. Secular voters lean heavily to the opposition and Haredim almost entirely to the coalition. Traditional voters lean coalition, but the traditional non-religious subgroup split significantly toward Yesh Atid and National Unity, which makes it the main persuadable segment.
findings.quant: Pooled IDI surveys (n=10,694 voters): Haredi 97% coalition; national-religious 80% coalition (opposition 10.5%); traditional 66.5% coalition; secular 74% opposition. Traditional non-religious: Likud 46%, Yesh Atid 17%, National Unity 14%. Likud voters: 57% traditional, 32% secular.
findings.title: Voting Patterns of Jews in the 2022 Elections by Religious Self-Definition
findings.relevance: Build a persuasion score from each locality's share of traditional, and especially traditional non-religious, adults (proxied from CBS religiosity data or past Likud and Yesh Atid co-strength). Treat Haredi and Hardal-heavy localities as having zero persuasion value.

findings.topic: Ethnic origin vs education and religiosity
findings.claim: Using surname-based classification of 440 small Jewish localities across ten elections, Dahan finds the Mizrahi-Ashkenazi gap in right-bloc voting swings widely between elections. The gap disappears or shrinks sharply once education and religiosity are controlled. Since about 2015, higher education predicts centre-left voting, and income also lowers the right-bloc vote.
findings.quant: 2022: right bloc about 61% in Mizrahi localities vs about 36% in Ashkenazi ones (a 25-point gap, the largest of the ten elections); the smallest gap was about 5 points in 2006. Caveat: Dahan's right-bloc definition reportedly differs from the standard one, and right-bloc shares are lower in Haredi localities and kibbutzim.
findings.title: Voting Gap by Origin (CESifo Working Paper No. 10857)
findings.relevance: Use education, religiosity and income, not ethnic-origin proxies, as locality covariates for bloc lean and persuadability. Localities that are rising in education are where the Change bloc's structural trend is improving.

findings.claim: In November 2022, the coalition parties won a majority in localities in CBS clusters 1-7 (excluding cluster 3, which holds many Arab localities), while the opposition won a majority only in clusters 8-10.
findings.quant: Clusters 1-7: coalition majority, and 72% support for the judicial overhaul. Clusters 8-10: opposition majority, and 54% oppose it. Survey (Smooha, 2021): 56.3% of self-identified Netanyahu supporters are Mizrahi.
findings.title: The Ascendance of Right-Wing Populism in Israel: An Ethno-Class Analysis
findings.venue: Reichman University (Libres blog; based on Nationalism and Ethnic Politics, 2025)
findings.relevance: Set the bloc tipping point at around clusters 7-8. Cluster 6-8 Jewish localities are where the Change bloc is competitive and should carry the highest combined persuasion and turnout weight.

findings.claim:
Analysis of 2019 locality and polling-station results shows sharp sorting:
- Likud peaked in low-cluster development towns, Blue and White in cluster 8-10 towns.
- Labor's remnant base was in kibbutzim.
- Yisrael Beytenu (YB) depended on Russian-speaking communities.
- The Druze vote moved sharply between parties from election to election.
findings.quant: Likud: Dimona 56%, Beit She'an 55% (clusters 4-5). Blue and White: Ramat HaSharon 56%, Hod HaSharon 54%; every cluster 8-10 city chose Blue and White. Labor: Niran 54%, Be'eri 49%. YB: Avshalom 35%, Nazareth Illit (Nof HaGalil) 21%; Kisra-Sumei fell from 41% to 21%. Haifa's left/right split 50/48.
findings.title: Demography is voting destiny: Ten takeaways from the 2019 election results
findings.relevance: Use these patterns to sanity-check locality classifications. Kibbutzim, including Gaza-envelope kibbutzim like Be'eri, are Change bloc strongholds with tiny electorates. Russian-speaking towns (Nof HaGalil, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Karmiel) are YB targets within the Change bloc.

findings.claim: Across five elections from 1984 to 2013, Tel Aviv's poorer southern neighbourhoods kept voting centre-right, the affluent north moved from the old centre-left to new centre parties, and the inner city grew steadily more centre-left. Big vote shifts coincided with demographic turnover.
findings.quant: Five general elections, 1984-2013; Labor, Likud, Meretz and Shas tracked by neighbourhood (no effect sizes in the abstract).
findings.title: Between electoral and urban geography: Voting patterns and socio-spatial dynamics in Tel Aviv
findings.relevance: Large cities (Tel Aviv, Jerusalem, Haifa, Be'er Sheva, Rishon LeZion) must be split to polling-station or statistical-area level. A whole-city average hides Change bloc turnout pockets and persuadable working-class neighbourhoods.

findings.claim: A Madlan analysis of 2022 results for every city over 50,000 residents found Rehovot still tracks the national result most closely. The cities least like the national result are Haredi, Arab, mixed or strongly sorted ones, including Tel Aviv and Jerusalem.
findings.quant: Rehovot's mean gap across the top 13 parties: 2.05 points (Likud 25.7 vs 23.4 nationally; Yesh Atid 23.1 vs 17.8). Next most similar: Petah Tikva, Haifa, Hadera, Netanya, Holon, Rosh HaAyin. Tel Aviv ranks 28th and Jerusalem 29th; Haifa is the only top-10 city where Yesh Atid beat Likud. Least similar: Umm al-Fahm, Modi'in Illit, Elad, Bnei Brak, Beitar Illit.
findings.year: 2026 (undated; published less than two months before the election)
findings.title: 'Israel's Ohio': These are the cities that have predicted election results
findings.relevance: Treat these balanced, large-electorate cities as Israel's swing states. A shift of a few points among their roughly 100,000-200,000 voters each moves national shares more than any single periphery town.

findings.claim: RZP dominated settlements east of the separation barrier and was strong west of it. Settlers are a small, young share of the electorate, and a notable part of RZP's vote came through double envelopes, mostly soldiers.
findings.quant: Nov 2022 RZP: 22% in all settlements; 59.7% east of the barrier; 22.4% west (31.5% excluding Beitar Illit and Modi'in Illit). Otzma/RZP range over five elections: 46.2-63.7% east, 17.9-27.0% west. Settlers are under 3.5% of eligible voters but cast about 6% of RZP's votes; 13.7% of RZP's votes were double-envelope.
findings.title: Tracking the Religious Zionist Party Bloc in the Settlements
findings.relevance: Give settlements east of the barrier near-zero priority. Secular settlements west of the barrier (e.g. Ariel) are Likud and YB territory, a possible minor YB persuasion target. Double-envelope votes mean soldier-heavy localities show understated home turnout.

findings.claim: In mixed cities the Arab vote splits among the three Arab lists and varies by city (Balad is strong in Lod, Hadash-Ta'al in Acre and Nof HaGalil). Haifa's Arab neighbourhoods give Hadash-Ta'al 25-45%. The Jewish parts of Lod, Ramla and Acre are among the most right-leaning large-city electorates.
findings.quant: 2022 citywide Arab-list shares (Arab share of population): Haifa (12%) Hadash-Ta'al 5.71%, Balad 2.85%, Ra'am 0.82%. Tel Aviv-Jaffa (5%) about 1.5% each for Hadash-Ta'al and Balad. Ramla (25%) Balad 6.0%, Ra'am 5.9%, Hadash-Ta'al 4.14%. Lod (31%) Balad 15.74%. Acre (32%) Hadash-Ta'al 11.7%, Ra'am 8.2%, Balad 7.47%. Nof HaGalil (29%) Hadash-Ta'al 16.87%.
findings.title: Arab Voting in 25th Knesset elections: Data Segmentation (Appendix)
findings.relevance: Model mixed cities at polling-station level, separating Arab and Jewish stations. Change bloc value lies in Haifa (centre-left Jewish neighbourhoods) and the Russian-speaking Jewish parts of Nof HaGalil and Ma'alot-Tarshiha (YB), not in Arab stations, except for the Ra'am scenario.

findings.topic: Arab, Bedouin and Druze voting by region (2022)
findings.claim: Zionist parties are now marginal in Arab localities, except among the Druze, where about 90% of votes went to Zionist lists. Ra'am dominates both Negev and northern Bedouin localities. Meretz still had a foothold in Christian Galilee villages, and Druze turnout is now below the Arab average.
findings.quant: Arab and Druze turnout 53.2% (2013-2022 average 55.9%); Umm al-Fahm 38.3%; Sakhnin 68.4%; Maghar 44%. Druze turnout averaged 48.7% in 2021-22 vs 55.9% in 2013-20. Ra'am: 73.9% in the Negev, 68.8% in northern Bedouin localities. Christian villages: Hadash-Ta'al 39.8%, Meretz 11.7%. Zionist parties won 14.3% in Arab localities (28.4% in April 2019). Druze localities: National Unity 30.4%, YB 18.3%, Meretz 14%, Likud 10.6%.
findings.title: Elections for the 25th Knesset: An Analysis of the Results in the Arab Sector
findings.relevance: Druze localities are the only non-Jewish localities where the Change bloc wins a majority (about 70% of 2022 votes went to its current parties or their predecessors). Weight them as Change bloc strongholds with large turnout headroom. Arab and Bedouin localities feed the Ra'am / Joint List calculus, not the Change bloc's own vote.

findings.topic: Druze turnout decline and home-candidate effect
findings.claim: Druze turnout has fallen steadily for three decades while national turnout recovered. Almost every party that placed a Druze candidate in a winnable list slot won the most votes in that candidate's home village. Voting has shifted from community-wide bloc voting to individual and local-candidate considerations.
findings.quant: Druze vs national turnout: 1996 76.8 vs 79.3; 1999 78.9 vs 78.7; 2003 64.2 vs 67.8; Sept 2019 53.2 vs 69.4. Examples: Fateen Mulla (Likud) moved Yarka from the Joint List to Likud in April 2019. Arab-list share of the Druze vote: 9.58% (1996), 3.75% (April 2019), 11.5% (2020).
findings.title: From a Community to a Society: Trends in Druze Voting Patterns in the Knesset Elections, 1996-2020
findings.venue: Bayan, Moshe Dayan Center, Tel Aviv University
findings.relevance: Add a home-village bonus for parties with a winnable-slot Druze candidate (e.g. Yashar with Kamil Abu Rokon). Druze localities also have about 6-12 points of turnout headroom against their 2003-2015 levels.

findings.topic: Druze vote elasticity: Nation-State Law and candidates (2015-2019)
findings.claim: Druze party choice swung sharply after the 2018 Nation-State Law and with candidate placement. Blue and White, which pledged to amend the law, won nearly half the Druze vote in September 2019. Parties gained or lost when Druze candidates were moved into or out of winnable slots, and turnout fell after the law.
findings.quant: Druze turnout: 57.7% (2015), 60.1% (April 2019), 54.5% (Sept 2019). Blue and White: 36% (April 2019) to 47.8% (Sept 2019). YB: 23.8% to 12.6% to 18.8%. Meretz: 2% to 15.8% to 3.2%. Home-village peaks: Blue and White 78.1% in Daliyat al-Karmel (Sept 2019, about 30 points above the Druze average); Meretz 64.8% in Beit Jann (April 2019, about 49 points above).
findings.title: The Druze Vote for the Twentieth, Twenty-First, and Twenty-Second Knesset Elections
findings.venue: Bayan, Moshe Dayan Center, Tel Aviv University
findings.relevance: Druze localities swing between elections, driven by candidates and grievances. Calibrate the home-village bonus at +30 points (range 20-50) and set a high persuasion elasticity for Change parties with credible Druze candidates and equality positions on the Nation-State Law.

findings.topic: Druze grievances 2023: Kaminitz law and planning
findings.claim:
The 2023 Druze protest was triggered by the Golan wind-turbine project but rooted in three grievances:
- Kaminitz-law fines and demolition orders for building on private agricultural land, felt most in Kisra and Isfiya.
- A planning and housing shortage.
- The Nation-State Law.
The author describes a strong sense of betrayal, aggravated by Ben Gvir. Druze voting for right-wing parties had already dropped after 2018.
findings.quant: Turnout fell from about 80% (1996, 1999) to about 50% (2021, 2022). Demand: a 5-year freeze on fines and demolitions while zoning plans are approved.
findings.title: The Druze Protest in the Summer of 2023
findings.venue: Bayan, Moshe Dayan Center, Tel Aviv University
findings.relevance: Issue agenda for Druze outreach: planning and zoning relief, a Kaminitz enforcement freeze, an equality clause. Prioritise Isfiya, Kisra-Sumei, Daliyat al-Karmel, Yarka, Beit Jann, Maghar and Peki'in.

findings.claim: A study of Druze electoral data from 2003 to 2022 attributes Druze voting to a mix of ideology (including reaction to the Nation-State Law), local socio-economic conditions and kinship networks, rather than to any single logic.
findings.quant: Elections 2003-2022; turnout and party-preference trends (no figures in the abstract).
findings.title: The Druze vote in Israel: between ideology, socioeconomic status, kinship, and the Nation-State Basic Law
findings.relevance: Supports Druze-specific covariates in the model: local SES, a kinship / local-candidate flag, and a time-varying ideological shock (2018 onward).

findings.claim: Zeedan suggested publicly that, despite anger over the Nation-State Law, Israeli Druze may be more inclined to back Netanyahu after Israel's 2025 military moves to protect Druze in southern Syria. This is an expert projection, not polling.
findings.quant: No numbers; expert commentary.
findings.authors: Rami Zeedan (University of Kansas news release)
findings.title: Expert can comment on Israeli moves to defend Syrian Druze, election outlook
findings.relevance: Add downside variance to the Druze Change share (range down to about 0.55). Commission a Druze-specific poll before committing heavy resources.

findings.claim: Kamil Abu Rokon, a Druze retired general and former Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT), joined Eisenkot's Yashar, which presented him as one of the most prominent Druze figures. Search-result snippets also said Eisenkot had pledged a Druze candidate in a winnable slot after touring Druze towns; his exact list slot was not verified.
findings.quant: List position not verified (one secondary report said #13; unconfirmed).
findings.title: Kamil Abu Rokon, former Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories, joins Eisenkot
findings.relevance: If he holds a winnable slot, apply the home-village bonus to his locality and a smaller community-wide boost to Yashar in Druze localities. Blue and White's Druze candidate, on a list polling about 1% and below the threshold, is a wasted-vote risk Yashar should counter-message.

findings.topic: Negev Bedouin turnout and polling-station access
findings.claim: About 40,000 eligible Bedouin voters live in unrecognised Negev villages, which have had no polling stations since the mid-1980s. They are assigned to stations in recognised towns by tribe name, regardless of distance. The Central Elections Committee rejected a 2022 petition for in-village stations. Turnout at these tribal stations is far below that of recognised Bedouin towns.
findings.quant: Stations are 5-65 km from home (Bir al-Bagar 65 km, Abda 60 km). Turnout 2022: national 70.63%, Arab 53.2%, recognised Negev Bedouin towns 56%, tribal stations 38% (2021: 67.4 / 44.6 / 45.8 / 32.4).
findings.authors: The Abraham Initiatives (policy paper to the Knesset Internal Affairs Committee)
findings.title: Ensuring Access to the Right to Vote for the Knesset among Residents of the Unrecognized Bedouin Villages in the Negev
findings.relevance: The roughly 18-point turnout gap shows transport is a binding constraint. It matters chiefly in the Ra'am-inclusive scenario, since Ra'am takes about 74% of the Negev Arab vote; direct Change bloc value is low.

findings.claim: In 2019 the Central Elections Committee chair, Justice Melcer, ruling on a Likud petition, held that a civil-society plan to bus about 15,000 Bedouin voters was politically motivated. The group (Zazim) could proceed only if it registered as a body active in the elections. Earlier that year a crowdfunded Zazim operation expected to transport 6,000-10,000 voters, using at least 40 minibuses and vans.
findings.quant: About 15,000 voters planned (Sept 2019); 6,000-10,000 expected (April 2019); distances up to about 70 km.
findings.title: Elections panel to send observers with cameras to problematic polling stations (incl. ruling blocking group from busing 15,000 Bedouins)
findings.relevance: Change bloc transport operations, such as for northern evacuees, Druze villages or the elderly, must run through the parties or registered bodies, and opponents will litigate. Budget legal compliance into turnout operations.

findings.claim: Israeli parties legally receive the voter register but may not pass it to third parties. Likud's Elector app combined the register with real-time election-day ground data on individual voters, polling stations (including each station's support level) and regions. Likud, YB, Labor and reportedly Shas used it. A 2020 flaw exposed the full register.
findings.quant: 6,453,254 voter records exposed (Feb 2020): names, ID numbers, addresses, plus phone numbers for some.
findings.title: In vast breach, Likud campaign leaks ID, phones, addresses of all Israeli adults
findings.relevance: Polling-station-level targeting from the register is standard practice. The Change bloc's playbook should turn locality priorities into polling-station walk and call lists using the register, while staying privacy-compliant: Israel's Privacy Protection Authority later found Elector, Likud and YB in breach.

findings.claim: In April 2019 a Likud-funded contractor placed about 1,200 activists with hidden body cameras as polling-committee representatives in Arab polling stations, organised as about 40 field coordinators each overseeing about 30 recruits. The firm claimed credit for low Arab turnout, but no causal effect was established. The budget roughly doubled for September 2019.
findings.quant: About 1,200 observers; Arab turnout 49.2% (April 2019) vs 63.8% (2015), national 68.5%; September budget about NIS 2 million.
findings.title: 'Operation Moral Standards': Inside Likud's election day Arab surveillance program
findings.relevance: Shows the Netanyahu bloc can staff thousands of polling-station posts. The Change bloc needs full committee and observer coverage in contested and mixed localities. Intimidation risk to Arab turnout affects the Ra'am-scenario math.

findings.claim: Before the September 2019 re-run, a coalition of 11 Arab civil-society groups (Coalition 17/9) ran door-to-door canvassing, Arabic leaflets, billboards and social media in 25 towns where April turnout had been especially low. Arab turnout rose from April to September, but the Joint List also reunited, so the campaign's effect cannot be separated.
findings.quant: Hundreds of volunteers; 25 targeted towns. Arab turnout 49.2% (April 2019) to 59.2% (Sept 2019), per Reichman appendix; internal pre-election poll projected 56%.
findings.title: Inside the grassroots drive to get Israel's Arabs to vote
findings.relevance: Arab turnout responds to list unity and organised mobilisation. Relevant to the Ra'am and Joint List components of the 61-seat math, and as a model for partner-led turnout drives in Druze and Christian localities.

findings.claim: In a 2019 survey experiment among Jewish voters for Blue and White, Likud, Meretz, Labor, Kulanu and YB, exposure to mock centre-left ads aimed at Arab citizens (equality, closing gaps, political partnership) did not significantly reduce support for the centre-left party. The equality and anti-racism ad was associated with a gain.
findings.quant: n=707 Jewish voters (iPanel, 15-20 Aug 2019); equality/anti-racism message about +11% support; other messages showed no significant change.
findings.authors: aChord Center (reported by The Abraham Initiatives)
findings.title: Center-left voters not deterred by messages that appeal to Arab public
findings.relevance: Weak evidence that Change parties can campaign in Druze, Christian and mixed-city Arab neighbourhoods without a measurable Jewish backlash. Treat as low-weight: single study, advocacy-linked.

findings.claim: The share of voters using special 'double envelope' arrangements (soldiers, hospital patients, prisoners, diplomats, polling staff) has grown. These votes are counted after regular ballots and are not attributed to home polling stations, which distorts locality turnout comparisons. They have shifted seats in past elections.
findings.quant: More than 200,000 double-envelope votes (2015-era report). 2013: Bayit Yehudi, Hatnua and Likud each gained a seat and the United Arab List lost one. 2022 figures by population group exist in the paper but were not retrieved.
findings.authors: Nir Atmor, Chen Friedberg, Ofer Kenig
findings.title: Special votes and voter turnout in Israel's 2022 elections
findings.relevance: Adjust locality turnout baselines upward in soldier- and reservist-heavy localities (settlements, national-religious moshavim, young suburbs). Expect 2026 double-envelope volume to be elevated by reserve mobilisation, and do not treat those localities' low home turnout as headroom.

findings.claim: Using the expanding range of Gaza rockets as a natural experiment (elections 1999-2009), the authors find localities inside rocket range voted more right-wing than comparable localities outside it. The mere threat of attack shifted votes.
findings.quant: Right-wing vote share 2-6 percentage points higher in localities within range.
findings.title: Terrorism and Voting: The Effect of Rocket Threat on Voting in Israeli Elections
findings.relevance: Historical prior: security-threatened localities (Gaza envelope, the north, the Ashkelon-Sderot belt) shift right by about 2-6 points. Compare against 2026 evidence of incumbent blame (D6-F32, D6-F34).

findings.topic: Local terror attacks and bloc vote
findings.claim: A terror attack in a locality within three months of an election raises that locality's right-bloc support. Effects spill beyond the locality and grow closer to election day. In left-leaning localities, attacks elsewhere tend to raise left-bloc support.
findings.quant: +1.35 percentage points in right-bloc share of the two-bloc vote per local attack within 3 months of the election.
findings.title: Are Voters Sensitive to Terrorism? Direct Evidence from the Israeli Electorate
findings.relevance: Use as a scenario shock: a late-campaign security incident would move affected localities about 1-2 points right. Keep an event-response rule in the playbook.

findings.claim: Re-examining Gaza rocket fire across elections 1999-2015, Elster finds the right-ward shift comes from actual exposure, measured by property-damage claims, rather than threat alone. Effects are larger for recent attacks, first exposure and proximity to Gaza.
findings.quant: +1,000 rocket-damage claims in a locality is associated with about +4 points in right-bloc vote share.
findings.title: Rockets and votes
findings.relevance: Scale the war-exposure prior by actual damage intensity, highest for Sderot, Kiryat Shmona, Metula, Shlomi and the Gaza-envelope kibbutzim, rather than a binary within-range flag.

findings.topic: Mismanaged war and punishing the incumbent
findings.claim: Using a regression discontinuity on almost 50 years of Israel National Election Studies, men just old enough to serve in the 1973 Yom Kippur War show lasting lower support for Labor, the incumbent that mismanaged it, than slightly younger cohorts. No such effect appears for well-managed wars.
findings.quant: Durable reduction in support for the incumbent among service-age cohorts (effect sizes not retrieved).
findings.title: War-time military service can affect partisan preferences
findings.relevance: After 7 October, reservist-heavy communities may punish Likud on security competence. Add an incumbent-blame term for localities with high reserve-duty exposure, especially traditional and national-religious ones with high service rates, partly offsetting D6-F29 to D6-F31.

findings.topic: Post-7 October panel evidence on political preferences
findings.claim: A four-wave panel of Jewish Israeli adults (early 2023 to late 2025) finds the war had weak, temporary effects on economic preferences but strong, persistent rightward shifts in political preferences across nearly all subgroups. Spatial variation in exposure to war violence corroborates this.
findings.quant: No magnitudes in the seminar abstract.
findings.title: The Effect of War on Economic and Political Preferences (seminar paper)
findings.venue: Bar-Ilan University Economics Department seminar, 11 May 2026
findings.relevance: A rightward shift in ideology need not mean votes for Likud: Yashar and Bennett offer right-of-centre security options inside the Change bloc. Persuasion messaging in exposed localities should be security-first.

findings.topic: Northern districts 2026: neglect and vote intention
findings.claim: A Midgam poll of Haifa and Northern District residents found a strong feeling that the state is abandoning the north, broad negative grades for the government's handling of the region, and an opposition lead with many undecided. In 2022 the coalition had narrowly led among northern residents.
findings.quant: Fieldwork 9 Apr 2026; 505 respondents; margin of error 5.7%. 65% say the state abandons the north; 70% give the government a 'poor' grade, including 31% of coalition voters. Vote intention: opposition 38%, coalition 26%, undecided 27%.
findings.title: N12 poll of northern residents (Haifa and Northern districts)
findings.relevance: Northern Jewish towns are 2026 persuasion targets, with a large undecided pool. 'Rebuild the north' messaging by Yashar and Together should go to Kiryat Shmona, Nahariya, Shlomi, Ma'alot, Karmiel, Safed and Tiberias. Small sample, so treat with caution.

findings.topic: Kiryat Shmona: displacement and political mood
findings.claim: Kiryat Shmona, a lower-income city of mainly Moroccan-origin Jews that has almost always voted Likud, had fewer than half its pre-war residents living there in April 2026. About one in four remaining residents depends on social services, the mayor publicly accused the government of neglect, and fighting resumed in March 2026.
findings.quant: Pre-7 October population about 25,000; about 10,000 present (April 2026).
findings.title: Israel's north: war-weary residents feel abandoned by government
findings.relevance: Large displacement implies depressed turnout at home polling stations unless evacuees are transported or special stations exist. These Likud-leaning displaced voters are reachable mainly through persuasion (blame for neglect), not get-out-the-vote. Add a displacement-adjusted electorate to the model.

findings.claim: In the delayed February 2025 northern municipal elections, the Likud-backed candidate in Kiryat Shmona finished second behind the incumbent mayor despite Netanyahu's endorsement. Eighty-three special stations around the country served evacuees who had not returned.
findings.quant: Turnout reported as 58.08% (internal figures inconsistent; about 52% implied); 5,205 votes cast in-city; 8,255 votes at the 83 special stations across the region.
findings.title: Kiryat Shmona: Likud candidate came second (local elections)
findings.relevance: A local signal that Likud brand loyalty in war-hit periphery towns has weakened. It also shows evacuee voting needs special arrangements; whether the CEC will provide them for the Knesset election is an open question.

findings.topic: Gaza envelope return and composition change
findings.claim: Government rehabilitation-authority figures show most Gaza-envelope evacuees have returned and newcomers have arrived, mostly in Sderot. The hardest-hit kibbutzim remain largely displaced.
findings.quant: 90% of evacuees returned (Sept 2025); some residents back in 42 of 47 evacuated communities; 2,500+ new residents since 7 October, mostly in Sderot; regional population about 65,000. Kibbutz Re'im 95% returned; Nahal Oz about one-third of families; Be'eri, Nir Oz and Kfar Aza largely displaced, some until 2027.
findings.title: 90% of Gaza envelope evacuees have returned home post-Oct. 7
findings.relevance: Displaced kibbutzim are Change bloc strongholds with tiny electorates. Their value is symbolic and tied to transport, not numerical. Sderot's newcomer inflow alters its baseline; treat its 2022 results as less reliable.

findings.claim: A July 2026 Maariv poll found opposition supporters more certain to vote than coalition supporters, reversing the 2022 enthusiasm pattern. Voters undecided between blocs were far less certain to vote.
findings.quant: Certain to vote: opposition 80%, coalition 72%, Arab-party supporters 82%, undecided between blocs 49%. Undecided about voting: coalition 8% vs opposition 1%.
findings.title: Who may stay home on election day? (Maariv poll)
findings.relevance: The Change bloc's base is already motivated, so marginal get-out-the-vote value is in low-propensity Change-leaning pockets (young voters, Druze, Russian-speaking YB voters, evacuees). Stated certainty overstates actual turnout, so discount it.

findings.topic: Reservists and the Haredi draft issue
findings.claim: In a December 2024 poll of reservists who fought in the war, a large majority rejected continued Haredi exemption, and many, including right-wing and religious reservists, said they would consider not voting for a party that backs an exemption law. About one in five favoured a Bennett party.
findings.quant: n=800 reservists (Dialogue Institute). 77% say exemptions are no longer affordable; 71% oppose an agreed exemption law; 60% would consider not voting for a party backing exemption (48% of right-wing, 35% of religious); 45% say such a law would reduce reserve motivation; about 20% intended to vote Bennett; Otzma 7%.
findings.authors: Dialogue Institute for the Shoulder to Shoulder campaign (reported by Jerusalem Post)
findings.title: Over three-quarters of IDF reservists say Israel can no longer exempt ultra-Orthodox from service
findings.relevance: The Haredi draft is the strongest wedge for persuading right-leaning reservist communities (national-religious moshavim, settlements west of the barrier, mid-cluster suburbs). The Change bloc should foreground it in those localities.

findings.claim: In Mizrahi development towns, national-level protest stayed within mainstream Zionist demands for resources, while local election campaigns were more militant and centred on competition with 1990s Russian-speaking immigrants. Place is central to periphery political identity.
findings.quant: Qualitative case study (no effect sizes).
findings.title: Between urban and national: Political mobilization among Mizrahim in Israel's 'development towns'
findings.relevance: Persuasion in development towns should be local and resource-focused (services, rebuilding, jobs) and delivered by trusted local figures. Russian-speaking and Mizrahi sub-communities in the same town need separate messages and messengers.

parameters.name: ses_turnout_gap_points
parameters.basis: D6-F02 (clusters 8-10 at 74.5% vs clusters 2-4 at 60.7% in non-Haredi Jewish localities, 2013) and D6-F01 (SES predicts turnout in 2022). Use for expected turnout and headroom by cluster.

parameters.name: gotv_min_net_bloc_margin
parameters.value: +20 points (Change share minus Netanyahu-bloc share among expected marginal voters)
parameters.basis: In a single national PR district, extra turnout helps the bloc only in proportion to (Change share minus Netanyahu share). D6-F05/F06 show Likud strongholds at about 45-56%, where raising turnout favours Netanyahu. Restrict get-out-the-vote spending to localities or polling stations above this margin.

parameters.name: locality_turnout_swing_amplitude_points
parameters.range: 0.3-9 (centre-left saturated cities about 0.3-1; Likud mid-size cities 3-7; peak 9)
parameters.basis: D6-F04 (Dimona +6.9, Beersheba +4.6, Tel Aviv +0.4) and D6-F05 (Likud share gains of +5 to +9 between consecutive elections).

parameters.name: bloc_enthusiasm_differential_2026_points
parameters.value: +3 turnout points in favour of opposition-leaning electorates
parameters.basis: D6-F38 (stated certainty 80% vs 72%), discounted because stated intent overstates turnout. D6-F03/F04 show the reverse gap of about 3-6 points in 2022, so allow for a possible return to that pattern.

parameters.name: secular_jewish_change_share
parameters.basis: D6-F07 (secular voters 74% opposition in 2022).

parameters.name: traditional_jewish_change_share
parameters.basis: D6-F07 (traditional 66.5% coalition; traditional non-religious about 31% Yesh Atid + National Unity). This is the main persuasion pool.

parameters.name: national_religious_change_share
parameters.basis: D6-F07 (opposition 10.5%; non-Hardal 12.5%, Hardal 2%). Upside via the draft issue (D6-F39).

parameters.name: haredi_change_share
parameters.basis: D6-F07 (97% coalition). Zero persuasion weight.

parameters.name: cluster_bloc_tipping_point
parameters.basis: D6-F09 (coalition majority in clusters 1-7, opposition majority in 8-10), D6-F10 (all cluster 8-10 cities chose Blue and White) and D6-F08 (education effect).

parameters.name: druze_change_bloc_share
parameters.basis: D6-F15 (2022 Druze localities: National Unity 30.4 + YB 18.3 + Meretz 14 + Yesh Atid 8.1 = 70.8%; Likud 10.6). Downside from D6-F20 (possible post-Sweida shift) and a wasted-vote risk from Blue and White's Druze candidate (D6-F21).

parameters.name: druze_home_village_candidate_bonus_points
parameters.basis: D6-F17 (Blue and White 78.1% in Daliyat vs 47.8% Druze average; Meretz 64.8% in Beit Jann vs 15.8% average) and D6-F16 (party with a winnable-slot candidate wins the home village). Apply to Yashar in Abu Rokon's locality if his slot is winnable (D6-F21).

parameters.name: arab_locality_zionist_party_share
parameters.basis: D6-F15 (14.3% in 2022). Change bloc share in Arab (non-Druze) localities about 0.08-0.10; higher in Christian villages (Meretz 11.7%).

parameters.name: negev_tribal_station_turnout_gap_points
parameters.basis: D6-F22 (tribal stations 38% vs recognised Bedouin towns 56% in 2022). Relevant only to Ra'am-inclusive scenarios (Ra'am about 74% of the Negev Arab vote, D6-F15); transport is legally constrained (D6-F23).

parameters.name: war_exposure_right_shift_prior_points
parameters.basis: D6-F29 (+2 to +6 within rocket range), D6-F30 (+1.35 per local attack within 3 months) and D6-F31 (about +4 per 1,000 damage claims). Scale by damage intensity.

parameters.name: incumbent_blame_offset_war_hit_localities_points
parameters.value: -5 (on Likud share vs 2022, in war-hit and reservist-heavy localities)
parameters.basis: D6-F32 (mismanaged-war cohort penalty), D6-F34 (north: opposition 38 vs coalition 26, where the coalition narrowly led in 2022), D6-F36 (Likud candidate second in Kiryat Shmona) and D6-F35 (neglect grievance). Net war effect = prior + offset. Some right-ward movement may go to Yashar or Together rather than Likud (D6-F33).

parameters.name: displacement_turnout_penalty_points
parameters.value: -10 for localities with under 60% of residents returned
parameters.basis: D6-F35 (Kiryat Shmona about 40% present in April 2026), D6-F36 (Feb 2025 municipal turnout about 52-58% with 83 special stations) and D6-F37 (Gaza envelope 90% returned, but Be'eri, Nir Oz and Kfar Aza largely displaced). Shrinks if the CEC provides special stations or transport runs.

parameters.name: special_vote_turnout_adjustment_points
parameters.value: +2 to the home-turnout baseline in soldier/reservist-heavy localities
parameters.basis: D6-F28 (double-envelope votes not attributed to localities and rising; more than 200,000 in 2015) and D6-F13 (13.7% of RZP's 2022 vote was double-envelope). Do not count this apparent shortfall as turnout headroom.

parameters.name: swing_city_weight_multiplier
parameters.basis: D6-F12 (Rehovot, Petah Tikva, Haifa, Hadera, Netanya, Holon and Rosh HaAyin track the national result) and D6-F05 (Rishon LeZion and Rosh HaAyin flipped plurality between 2019 and 2020). Apply to large balanced cities when combining persuasion and turnout scores.

parameters.name: settlement_east_of_barrier_priority
parameters.basis: D6-F13 (RZP 59.7% east of the barrier; Otzma/RZP 46-64% across 2019-22). Low Change share and a small electorate.

open_questions: The shared web-search budget (200 calls per turn) ran out partway through this desk, so these strands are thin or missing and need a follow-up run: Yesh Atid's volunteer and field model and its effectiveness; Russian-language media campaigns and 2022 vote shares among former-Soviet immigrants (no source found after 2015); Shas and Likud election-day machines beyond anecdotes; the CBS peripherality index and its link to bloc vote; ecological-inference studies of vote transfers.

I could not find or verify the Hebrew-language resources named in the brief ('Kolot Nodedim', 'Hamadad', IDI or Haaretz interactive electoral maps), or locality-level electoral-geography work by Arnon Soffer, Gad Barzilai or Shlomo Hasson. A Hebrew-language search pass is recommended.

Will the Central Elections Committee provide special polling stations or transport for displaced northern residents (e.g. Kiryat Shmona) in the 27 October Knesset election, as it did with 83 special stations in the February 2025 municipal elections? This decides whether displacement is modelled as a turnout penalty or a transport opportunity.

No randomised get-out-the-vote or canvassing field experiment conducted in Israel was found. Effect sizes for field tactics must be borrowed from foreign evidence (other desks) and discounted for Israel's in-person, polling-station-bound voting.

Direction of the Druze vote after Sweida (2025): no 2026 polling found. Also unverified are Kamil Abu Rokon's list slot and home locality, and whether the Likud, YB and Democrats lists place Druze candidates in winnable slots. All of these determine the home-village bonuses.

Dahan's right-bloc definition (reported secondhand to include YB and exclude Shas) and the 2022 special-vote breakdown by population group in Atmor, Friedberg and Kenig (2025) could not be confirmed from full texts.

No locality-level analysis of political change in Gaza-envelope kibbutzim, reservist-heavy communities or the evacuated northern towns between 2022 and 2026 was found beyond the N12 regional poll and the Kiryat Shmona municipal result. Polling by community type is needed.
The Israel Hayom 2022 Likud targeting list (D6-F06) is based on a search-result excerpt; the full article could not be fetched (HTTP 403).
